politicalStatus.value: Federal Dominion under the British Crown

governments.value: Crown, Governor General and Privy Council; Parliament with Senate and House of Commons

descriptions.value: The 1867 union created a federal Dominion. Ottawa was its statutory seat of government. This core describes federal institutions, not a claim that every mapped territory had joined Confederation or that Indigenous sovereignty was extinguished.

This interval ends with Canadian Confederation on 31 March 1949.

governments.value: Formal separation of executive, legislative and judicial branches

descriptions.value: The 1917 constitution established a federal republican framework. This core describes formal institutions, without claiming that constitutional rights guaranteed competitive democracy or uniform practical authority during revolutionary consolidation. Later amendments and exhaustive officeholders remain uncurated.

By the early 1940s the political system centred on a strong civilian president and an official ruling party. Formal separation of powers should not be confused with equal effective authority or open electoral competition. This context is confined to the later period; current party arrangements are excluded.

sources.title: Canadian Parliamentary Institutions — historical development
sources.usage: Read historical body and chronology, especially 1791 separate Upper/Lower Canada, maritime colonies, 1867 union effective 1 July, and 1934 Newfoundland suspension. The broad chronology oversimplifies Newfoundland’s 1931 statute applicability; original section 10 controls instead. Modern officeholder rules and representation counts excluded.

sources.title: Constitution Act, 1867 — Union, executive and Parliament
sources.usage: Read sections 3, 5, 9–17 and historical notes. Supports Dominion, executive Crown/Governor General/Privy Council, Ottawa and Senate/Commons. Current amended chamber sizes, modern province list and 1982 rights not projected backwards.

sources.title: Statute of Westminster 1931 — original enacted text
sources.usage: Read full original body by public HTTP download: dated 11 December 1931, sections 2–4 remove repugnancy restriction and require request/consent for UK legislation; section 7 preserves British North America Acts amendment exception. Section 10 excludes Newfoundland from automatic adoption of sections 2–6.

sources.title: Responsible Government, 1855–1933
sources.usage: Read complete body in isolated downloaded HTML. Responsible government in domestic matters, imperial external affairs, Assembly and Executive Council; war/postwar politics. Specific officeholder term precision not used.

sources.institution: Memorial University of Newfoundland / Jeff A. Webb
sources.title: The Commission of Government, 1934–1949
sources.usage: Read complete downloaded body: sworn 16 February 1934, governor chairs six appointed commissioners, no election or legislature, major policies/budget require Dominions Office permission; Dominion in name. Confederation official 31 March 1949.

sources.institution: Manatū Taonga — New Zealand Ministry for Culture and Heritage
sources.title: Becoming a dominion
sources.usage: Read body stating Dominion became distinguishing label for Newfoundland and other self-governing administrations in 1907. The precise New Zealand 26 September proclamation is not incorrectly transferred to Newfoundland.

sources.institution: Danish Ministry of Foreign Affairs / Royal Danish Embassy Japan
sources.title: Greenland — History and culture
sources.usage: Read historical paragraphs: Danish colonial period until 1953, constitutional county status in 1953, home rule only 1979; wartime communications suspended. Modern 2009 autonomy and current capital/status omitted. Colonial coverage restricted to 1878–1900, before wartime complication.

sources.title: Greenland and the UN: Colony or not a colony
sources.usage: Read historical body: 1953 integration into Denmark, elected regional assemblies consulted but constitution not put to direct Greenland vote, contested decolonisation interpretation and 1954 UN declaration. County integration does not establish independence or unanimous popular consent.

sources.institution: Library of Congress Federal Research Division
sources.title: Mexico: A Country Study (1996) — historical setting and constitutional history
sources.usage: Downloaded and extracted full PDF; read printed pp. 11–19, 31–41, 232–236 (PDF 67–75, 87–97, 300–304): colonial viceroy/audiencia and limited distant authority; 1810–21 civil war/1815 royalists; Díaz direct/indirect personalist rule under 1857 formal institutions; 1917 constitutional separation and early-1940s dominant-party presidency. Date errors and insulting period rhetoric excluded; modern 1990s membership counts/economic facts not projected.

sources.title: México bajo Porfirio Díaz, 1876–1911
sources.usage: Read full Spanish exhibition body, Porfirio Díaz en 1867 section: explicit first presidency ending 30 November 1880; inclusive end represented by exclusive 1 December 1880. Later body records 1884 return; editorial leader starts 1885 and ends before 1910 revolutionary period. Repeated reelections and suppression of dissent documented. González interval is not assigned to Díaz.

sources.title: The Constitution of 1917
sources.usage: Read exhibition body with original constitutional provenance: proclaimed 5 February 1917, government and Mexico City capital, Church/state separation and social rights. Editorial dossier starts 1918 to avoid conflating proclamation with implementation; amendments and practical authority remain explicitly partial.

sources.institution: Instituto Nacional de Antropología e Historia / Archivo General de la Nación
sources.title: Bando of Viceroy Félix María Calleja, 22 September 1815
sources.usage: Read full primary transcription including official titulature, palace of Mexico date and archival references AGN bandos vol. 28 exp.67 f.145. Documents viceroy/governor/captain-general and Real Audiencia presidency on that day; office tenure is not inferred beyond attestation.

sources.title: Federal legislation and Canadian territories — Rupert’s Land charter and admission
sources.usage: Read historical body including 1670 charter extracts, Crown-reserved allegiance/dominion, HBC proprietary/trading authority and 1870 admission. Crown/company grants are represented as colonial claims, not proof that Indigenous nations surrendered sovereignty or territory.

sources.title: Louisiana Purchase Treaty (1803)
sources.usage: Read primary transcript and introduction: Article I recalls Spanish retrocession agreement at San Ildefonso on 1 October 1800, then French cession to US; transfer clauses distinguish title/treaty and possession. Profile stops at 1 October 1800 rather than guessing post-treaty legal or actual administration.

sources.title: Louisiana Territory Officially Transferred
sources.usage: Read article body: New Orleans Spanish/French Cabildo and Spanish transfer 30 November 1803, Upper Louisiana retained Spanish control to March 1804. The article’s inconsistent sentence on US possession ten days after 20 December is excluded, and no uniform post-1800 transfer mapping accepted.
